label: paragraph_title
text: Hongkong, Monday, July 6, 1925.

label: text
text: The extension of the cars to Whitty Street—right through the densely-packed Chinese quarter of the city—must be conceded an event—of no slight importance. The tram workers were the first to come out—without giving notice, it is again emphasised—paralysing in a second an arm of service much used by Chinese and foreigners. The limited service begun a week ago has had a moral effect amongst those living in the Wanchai district; and the same is likely to be the case with those living in the central and western district. Foreigners with spare time on their hands, might do worse than take a ride to Whitty Street and back to town. For one thing they will obtain a refreshing and cooling, ride; they will help to fill rather empty cars and encourage the Tramway Co., but above all they will show to those who raise wondering eyes to the sight of passing cars, or stand and smile in a knowing manner, that the foreigner is capable of taking his troubles—his unsought troubles—smilingly.

Tokyo, July 8.—Owing to financial depression, causing increasing discount against the Government, the Peraler made a statement that after now proving that the former Government's policy was responsible and saying no intended continuing the pre-
I am an American of twelve years' residence in Hongkong and China, with great respect and admiration for the Chinese. I admire your character, your judgment, the sanctity of your pledged word, your love of bodily peace and tranquillity of mind. I have no ulterior motive in making this plea to you for I have not a single cent invested outside of my own country and the present state of affairs has not affected my mode of living in the slightest. I merely ask you to pause and compare your present security of mind, body and property with the possibilities in the future if Bolshevism gains control of China.

label: text
text: You are now living under the fairest government in the world. This is no ill-considered statement and if you have visited other countries and studied their government you must admit its truth. There is no place under the sun where anyone has as much personal liberty as here. You can carry on your life and trade with the minimum of governmental regulation and restriction. You are guaranteed and you receive absolute justice without a suspicion of discrimination on account of race, creed, colour, or condition of life. Your customs and religion are respected without interference of any nature. This colony is administered by a set of men who have made a life study of the science of government; without question they are men of education, probity and sound judgment. They and their predecessors have turned a barren rock into a beautiful healthy spot with a superb system of roadways, excellent sanitation, adequate schools and free hospitals. In all of this you share equally yet taxes are so low that they are comparatively negligible.

label: text
text: And yet you listen to cries of British Imperialism! Fraternalism if you will, paternalism if you must, but not Imperialism in an invidious sense. Do you think you might obtain equal benefits in republics such as France or the United States? Though a citizen of the latter country, I am regretfully forced to tell you that you would not; it is not that the American friendship for China is not sincere, or that you would be discriminated against, but not even its own people have the privileges you receive here. If this be true, what are you doing to assure a continuation of your unique condition? You are alive to the fact that this community cannot exist without trade, principally with South China, and if Bolshevism conquers in Canton, depression will follow here with destitution, misery and want in its wake. The burden will fall on you far more heavily than on the foreigner who can transfer his sphere of activity elsewhere.

label: text
text:
There is not a single thing that the Hongkong Government or a member of this community can do to settle the Shanghai or Shameen incidents. The unprovoked walk-out cannot assist the settlement, cannot hasten or retard it. Except for a slight inconvenience to some foreigners, this strike appears to be principally directed against you; surely you must realize that in many ways you are the ultimate losers. The time has come for a show of sanity; a firm courageous word from you will stop this silly procedure at once. The Government has guaranteed you safety and you are convinced that you can trust its guarantee. You know or you can easily find out who these cowardly agitators are you alone can curb their activities; you can kill the silly canards passed among the ignorant here and widely quoted in China. Are you willing to protect your future? Your choice is clear—do you wish peace and prosperity or chaos and penury?
Do not listen to hard-brained missionaries; pay no attention to irresponsible, poorly posted politics in America and France.

label: paragraph_title
text: OBITUARY.

label: text
text: It is with regret that the "China Mail" records the death of Inspector Peter Angus, an efficient and courteous officer, exceedingly popular with his fellow officers and men and well-known and respected by many other than police circles. The respect in which he was held was evidenced by the large attendance at the funeral yesterday afternoon. Death took place early in the morning.

label: text
text: Inspector Angus had been in Hospital for two months and underwent an operation two weeks ago for internal trouble. His condition had given cause for anxiety but the news of his death came as a great shock to many. His age was 51.

label: text
text: The greatest sympathy is felt for Mrs. Angus, daughter, and three sons, a factor which adds even greater poignancy to their bereavement being that arrangements had been made by which the family was to leave for Home very shortly. The deceased's pensionable service was complete a year ago.

label: text
text: The late Inspector Angus was a native of Edinburgh and at the age of 23 he left the Glasgow police for the Hongkong Force. At the time of his death he was Divisional Inspector of the Water Police Station, Tsimshatsui.

label: text
text: The Rev. G. R. Lindsay, of St. Andrew's Church, Kowloon, officiated at the funeral yesterday afternoon when the coffin, draped in the Union Jack, was drawn to the cemetery by a number of police sergeants and followed by large contingents of European, Indian, and Weihaiwei members of the Hongkong Police Force. At Happy Valley the procession was joined by other police officers and civilians.

label: paragraph_title
text: GOLD MEDAL.

label: text
text: HIGHEST REWARD FOR AMUNDSEN.

label: text
text: Amundsen and his companions have arrived by air from Horten. They were accorded a most enthusiastic welcome. The Polar fliers' aeroplane was escorted to Oslo by five Army and five Navy aeroplanes all of which descended into the harbour to the accompaniment of salutes of the fortress.

label: text
text: A Norwegian cruiser, vessels of the British Naval Squadron now visiting the port and steamers in harbour sirened the people aboard. Crowds ashore cheered, the streets of the city were gaily decorated.

label: text
text: Amundsen and his party received a cordial reception from President Storting, chairman of the Oslo Municipality.

label: text
text: The aviators subsequently drove to the Palace where the King presented Amundsen with a gold medal for a patriotic deed, the highest distinction only held by two living persons.

label: text
text: The other members of the party were decorated with the order of Stoslay.

label: text
text: Earl Crawford, the former Cabinet Minister, speaking at Gillingham, said the time had come for the British Government to give clear and unmistakable warning to Russia that continued organisation of anti-British attacks in China, India and elsewhere would result in the breaking of Anglo-Russian diplomatic relations.

label: text
text: Britain was. tiring of these underhand, underground attacks and was determined to end them.
